stem: Before cleaning and cannulating a client's AV fistula for hemodialysis, which access assessment should the nurse perform?

options.A: Inspect the access, auscultate for the usual bruit, and palpate for the usual thrill so changes in access function are identified before use.
options.B: Inspect the access and palpate for the usual thrill, then proceed with cleaning and cannulation without auscultating if the thrill feels unchanged.
options.C: Inspect the access and auscultate for the usual bruit, then proceed with cleaning and cannulation without palpating if the bruit sounds unchanged.
options.D: Check the client's blood pressure and radial pulse, then clean and cannulate the access if systemic circulation appears stable.

rationale: The National Kidney Foundation states that the dialysis care team should check a fistula or graft every time the client comes for treatment and should look, listen, and feel the access before the skin is cleaned. The team uses a stethoscope to listen for the bruit and palpates for the thrill, both of which reflect blood flow through the access. Therefore A is correct. B and C each omit one component of the recommended local access assessment. D substitutes systemic circulation findings for direct assessment of the fistula and therefore can miss access dysfunction before cannulation.
educational_objective: Before hemodialysis cannulation, assess an AV fistula by inspecting it, auscultating the bruit, and palpating the thrill before skin preparation so access-function changes are recognized before use.
source_document_title: Inserting Your Own Needles for Dialysis (Self-Cannulation) Is Your Right!; Hemodialysis Access
source_locator: Inserting Your Own Needles for Dialysis > It only takes a minute to see if your fistula or graft is working well: the dialysis care team should check the fistula/graft every treatment; look, listen, and feel before the skin is cleaned; use a stethoscope to listen to the bruit and palpate the thrill. Hemodialysis Access > Keeping your access working: check blood flow by feeling for the thrill and report absence or change because access dysfunction can reduce delivered dialysis.
source_claim_supported: A fistula or graft should be assessed before skin cleaning/cannulation at each hemodialysis treatment by inspection, auscultation of the bruit, and palpation of the thrill.

supporting_sources.locator: Keeping your access working: the dialysis care team checks the access often; check blood flow by feeling for the vibration/thrill and report absence or change because poor access function can reduce the amount of dialysis received.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Changes in the access thrill can indicate dysfunction and require evaluation.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed pp. 14 and 46–49: manage the care of a client receiving hemodialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy; recognize signs and symptoms of client complications and intervene; apply knowledge of nursing procedures and psychomotor skills when caring for a client with an alteration in body systems.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — pre-cannulation AV fistula assessment for hemodialysis
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four options to remove absolute-word cueing and the uniquely-long keyed answer, converted the distractors into realistic incomplete access-assessment patterns, and remapped the item to the more direct NCSBN Physiological Adaptation hemodialysis activity statement.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Hemodialysis vascular access — AV fistula pre-cannulation assessment
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies the exact pre-cleaning, pre-cannulation phase and asks one access-assessment question.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — includes all three NKF-recommended components: look, listen for bruit, and feel for thrill; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — inspection and thrill palpation are appropriate but omitting auscultation leaves the assessment incomplete.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — inspection and bruit auscultation are appropriate but omitting thrill palpation leaves the assessment incomplete.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — systemic blood pressure and pulse can be relevant to dialysis care but do not replace direct assessment of access blood flow.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — only A performs the complete directly sourced pre-cannulation access assessment.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B and C each omit a required local component; D substitutes systemic findings for local access assessment.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the keyed answer is not uniquely long and no option contains a keyed-only absolute-word pattern.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation directly includes management of clients receiving hemodialysis.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether a normal thrill alone or bruit alone could reasonably permit cannulation; NKF explicitly instructs the care team to look, listen, and feel before cleaning at each treatment, so A remains uniquely complete.
